---
title: "Quiz: images in frequency space"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why does the discrete Fourier transform lose no information about an image?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is a change of basis. An image of $N$ pixels becomes $N$ wave amounts: the same vector written in another coordinate system, as when you describe a point by different axes. Nothing is thrown away, and you can always go back exactly. (In formulas: $X = Fx$ with an invertible matrix $F$, $F^{-1} = \tfrac1N F^*$ because the waves are orthogonal, and $x = F^{-1}X$ recovers the image.)
:::

---

**Q2.** In the centred spectrum of a micrograph, where do you find the information about (a) the overall brightness, (b) the broad shape of the cell, (c) the fine texture and the noise?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) The single centre coefficient, frequency $(0, 0)$: it is $N^2$ times the mean grey level. (b) Close to the centre: low frequencies. (c) Far from the centre: high frequencies. Note that sharp *real* edges are high-frequency as well, so a low-pass filter that removes noise also blurs edges.
:::

---

**Q3.** An image has a regular pattern of horizontal stripes (lines running left–right), 8 pixels apart, in a 256 × 256 image. Where are the bright dots in its spectrum?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The brightness changes when you move *up and down*, not left–right. How many cycles fit in the image?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On the **vertical** axis through the centre, at $256/8 = 32$ cycles: the pair $(u, v) = (0, \pm 32)$. The dots are perpendicular to the stripes, and come in a mirror pair because the image is real.
:::

---

**Q4.** You blur an image by convolving with a $31 \times 31$ Gaussian kernel. How else could you compute the same result, and why might it be faster?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
By the convolution theorem: FFT the image and the (zero-padded) kernel, multiply the spectra, inverse FFT. Direct convolution costs about $31^2 \approx 960$ multiplications per pixel; the FFT route costs $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ per pixel. (The Gaussian is also separable: a 31-tap pass along rows then along columns, 62 multiplications per pixel.) Beware: the FFT treats the image as periodic, so pad the image to avoid wrap-around at the border.
:::

---

**Q5.** You reduce a photo of a brick wall to a quarter of its size by keeping every 4th pixel in each direction. A strange wavy pattern appears that is not on the wall. What happened, and how do you prevent it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Aliasing.** The new grid can only hold frequencies up to a quarter of the original Nyquist frequency; the fine brick pattern is above that and folds back as a false, coarser pattern (moiré). Low-pass filter (blur) the image first, so that what the coarse grid cannot represent is removed before sampling.
:::

---

**Q6.** A detector adds a faint regular stripe to every image. Should you remove it with a low-pass filter or a notch filter? Why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A **notch**. The stripe is a single wave, so in the spectrum it is one isolated pair of dots; zeroing just those (and their immediate neighbours) removes the stripe and leaves everything else. A low-pass filter would also remove every real structure finer than the stripe.
:::

---

**Q7.** A cell sits in the left half of an image. In a second image, the same cell has moved 30 pixels to the right (on the same flat background). How do the two magnitude spectra $|X_{u,v}|$ compare? What has changed in the full spectrum?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Shifting a wave slides its peaks along. Does it make the wave stronger or weaker?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The magnitude spectra are the same. Moving the image shifts every wave in it, which changes *where* its peaks are (its **phase**), not how strong it is. The magnitude spectrum describes *what* structures are present, not *where*; the position is stored in the phases. (Strictly this holds exactly for a shift that wraps around the image, which on a flat background is the same thing.)
:::
